abstract: This AI Economics Brief synthesizes 2025 research on AI's labor market impacts across predictions, capabilities, diffusion, and employment effects. Expert forecasts predict slower white-collar job growth (2% vs. 6.8% historical trend through 2030), with one in four experts expecting net job losses. Early labor market evidence is mixed: while AI capabilities continue advancing exponentially and adoption is accelerating (reaching 9.7% of US firms by August 2025), measured employment effects remain limited overall, though entry-level workers in AI-exposed jobs show a 13% relative employment decline.
keyFindings: Forecasting Research Institute experts predicted median 2% white-collar job growth from January 2025 to December 2030, significantly below the 6.8% pre-existing trend, with 25% of experts foreseeing net job losses.
AI adoption among US firms more than doubled from 3.7% in fall 2023 to 9.7% in early August 2025, with variation by sector (Information sector at ~25% vs. Accommodation and Food Services at ~2.5%).
Field experiments in online retail (October 2025) estimated causal effects of AI integration ranging from 0% to 16.3% in sales, with approximately $5 annual incremental value per consumer.
Brynjolfsson et al. (August 2025) found a 13% relative decline in employment among early-career workers in AI-affected jobs since generative AI adoption, validated across UK and US data.

Humlum and Vestergaard (August 2025) found no measurable effects on earnings or hours from AI adoption using Danish government employment records, suggesting job losses and creation may be roughly balanced.
methodology: This is a curated literature review synthesizing multiple 2025 studies on AI's labor market impacts. Key studies include: (1) Forecasting Research Institute expert panel survey (November 2025) on white-collar job projections; (2) Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey data on AI adoption rates; (3) Fang et al. field experiment in online retail (October 2025) over six months in 2023-2024; (4) Humlum and Vestergaard analysis using Danish government employment records (August 2025); (5) Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen study (August 2025) validated with UK LinkedIn/job-posting data and US résumé data. The brief also references METR capability research (March 2025), OpenAI GDPVal evaluations (September-December 2025), and Dallas Fed analysis (June 2025).
qualifiers: Authors note 'extraordinarily wide' range of predictions on AI's economic impacts with 'significant disagreement' between Silicon Valley, financial markets, and economists. Dallas Fed analysis states there is currently 'little empirical evidence' to support extreme scenarios. Authors caution that 'it remains unclear how' AI capability improvements translate to economic impacts and that 'benchmarks often lead to overconfident predictions about their economic impact.' They note data from Humlum & Vestergaard ends before late 2024 when US and UK studies begin detecting reduced junior hiring, potentially explaining divergent findings. Brynjolfsson et al. findings limited to early-career workers in AI-affected jobs; effects for more experienced workers differ. Fang et al. results specific to consumer-facing online retail workflows. AI adoption remains 'in its early stages' overall.
